newsitem.title: GERMANY: German print media lose ad money to TV and mail.
newsitem.headline: German print media lose ad money to TV and mail.

text.p: German newspapers and magazines lost ground in advertising income to television and direct mailing in 1996, Germany's central advertising association (ZAW) said on Tuesday.

While mass media as a whole posted a mild 3.1 percent gain in advertising income last year in Germany, an increasingly cut-throat market did not allow all to share the gain equally, the ZAW said in a statement.

"The advertising year 1996 brought mixed results for the media," it said. "Net advertising income reached a record 37.5 billion marks ($22 billion), but the individual media profited in different ways from it and some even saw a drop in income."
Although newspapers remained the most important medium for advertising in 1996 with 10.7 billion marks in net ad income, the figure marked a drop of 43 million marks from 1995.

Magazines shared a similar fate, witnessing a 100 million mark drop in advertising revenues to 3.4 billion marks. The ZAW said this was largely attributable to stiff competition and a price war in the print advertising industry.
Net advertising income in television rose 555 million marks, or 8.7 percent, to 6.9 billion marks.
Although the figures kept TV in second place among German advertising media, the ZAW said the modest growth in 1996 reflected a weakening of the medium's power to draw ads.
"The growth rate of 8.7 percent was the first time in 10 years that it was in single digits," the ZAW said.
Direct mail maintained its steady growth of the last few years, with Deutsche Post AG reporting a boost in advertising income of 400 million marks to 5.7 billion marks for 1996.
Internet advertising had been a disappointment, the ZAW said, growing far more slowly than industry experts expected.
The association said Germany remains the largest European advertising market, and the third largest in the world behind the United States and Japan.

Looking to 1997, the ZAW said the years of soaring growth for German advertising are over and the industry can only expect a slight increase in ad expenditure of 2.4 percent to 56.4 billion marks for the current year.

The ZAW said it expected little change in the advertising market this year. It expected a rise of around one billion marks in net advertising income, which excludes distribution costs and media agency fees, to 38.5 billion marks in 1997.

The ZAW monitors the posted figures of the German advertising industry and presents results for the market annually. Included in its data are spending on ad production, ad agencies and the industry as a whole. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
